result: The study analyzed 85,854,176 deaths in the USA from 1980 to 2016. Cardiorespiratory diseases accounted for 48.1% of all deaths (mostly cardiovascular), cancers for 23.2%, and injuries for 6.8% (two-thirds unintentional).
evaluation: Claims C9-C14 provide descriptive statistics directly from the dataset stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Table 1. The numbers are internally consistent and represent straightforward data summaries with no complex inference required.

result: All-cause mortality exhibited 12-month seasonality in most age groups for both sexes, with notable exceptions. Males aged 35-44 showed 6-month periodicity. Females aged 5-14 and 25-34 showed no significant seasonality. Seasonality persisted in older ages throughout 1980-2016 but largely disappeared after the late 1990s in children aged 0-4 years (both sexes) and women aged 15-24 years.
evaluation: Claims C15-C20 describe wavelet analysis results shown in Figures 1-2 with reported p-values. The statistical methodology is appropriate for detecting periodic patterns in time series data. The temporal changes are clearly visible in the figures and supported by statistical testing.

result: Cause-specific mortality showed distinct seasonal patterns by age. In older adults (≥65-75 years), deaths from all causes except intentional injuries and substance use disorders were seasonal (p<0.06). Cardiorespiratory diseases and respiratory infections exhibited seasonality throughout the life-course except for specific young age groups. Cancer deaths showed consistent seasonality only after age 55. Substance use disorders and maternal conditions showed no consistent seasonality.
evaluation: Claims C21-C25, C30-C32 describe cause-specific seasonality patterns supported by Figures 3-10 and supplements with reported p-values. The age-specific patterns are clearly documented in the wavelet analyses. The statistical thresholds (p<0.06, p<0.05) are consistently applied across analyses.

result: Injury deaths were seasonal from childhood through age 44 in women and through age 64 in men (p<0.09). Unintentional injuries drove seasonality in females, while both unintentional and intentional injuries were seasonal in males at most ages, except intentional injuries were not seasonal in males below 15 years and above 85 years.
evaluation: Claims C26-C29 describe injury-specific seasonality patterns shown in Figures 7-8 and supplements with reported p-values. The sex-specific differences and age-specific exceptions are clearly documented in the figure supplements. The patterns are consistent with the overall analytical approach.

result: The timing of mortality peaks varied by age and cause. In adults ≥45 years, death rates peaked in December-February and were lowest in June-August. Cardiorespiratory disease deaths were consistently highest in January-February and lowest in July-August across all ages. In contrast, males aged 5-34 years showed all-cause mortality peaks in June-July, and injury deaths generally peaked in summer for those below age 45.
evaluation: Claims C2, C7, C33-C35 describe center of gravity analysis results shown in Figure 11 and supplements. The opposing seasonal patterns (winter peaks for older adults/cardiorespiratory diseases vs. summer peaks for young adults/injuries) are clearly demonstrated. The circular statistics methodology is appropriate for identifying timing of peaks.

result: The seasonality of all-cause mortality in adults ≥45 years is driven by cardiorespiratory diseases and injuries, while the summer mortality peak in adolescents and young adults is driven by injury deaths.
evaluation: Claims C3 and C8 make causal attributions about drivers of seasonality. These are supported by the cause-specific analyses in Figures 5-7 showing that the seasonal patterns of specific causes align with all-cause patterns in the respective age groups. The inference is reasonable given the data.

result: For ages ≥45 years, the percent difference in death rates between peak and minimum months did not vary across climate regions and did not change substantially from 1980 to 2016 (declined by less than 8 percentage points, p>0.1).
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C36 describe temporal and geographic stability of seasonal mortality magnitude shown in Figures 12 and 17. The statistical testing (p>0.1 for temporal trend) and the small magnitude of change (<8 percentage points) support the conclusion of stability. The regional consistency is clearly shown in Figure 17.

result: In younger ages, seasonal mortality differences declined substantially from 1980 to 2016. Males aged 5-24 years showed declines exceeding 25 percentage points (p<0.01), driven by declining summer-winter differences in injury deaths. In children under 5, the decline was 13 percentage points for boys (p<0.01) but only 5 for girls (p=0.12), resulting from declining winter-summer differences in cardiorespiratory deaths and increasing summer-winter differences in injury deaths.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 describe temporal changes in young age groups shown in Figure 12 and supplements with reported p-values. The sex-specific differences and cause-specific decomposition are clearly documented. The statistical significance is appropriately reported, including the non-significant result for girls (p=0.12).

result: Seasonality of all-cause mortality largely disappeared after the 1990s in children under five years.
evaluation: Claim C6 is directly supported by the wavelet analyses in Figures 1-2 showing loss of 12-month periodicity after the late 1990s in the 0-4 age group. This is a major finding regarding temporal changes in child mortality patterns.

result: All-cause mortality peaks and minima were consistent across different climate regions, indicating seasonality is largely independent of geography. Above age 45, there was little inter-region variation in percent seasonal mortality difference despite large temperature variations between regions (e.g., 13°C difference between Northeast and Southeast, both peaking in February for ages 65-74).
evaluation: Claims C41-C44 describe geographic consistency shown in Figures 13-17. The center of gravity analyses demonstrate similar timing across regions, and Figure 17 shows minimal variation in seasonal magnitude despite temperature differences. The specific example (C44) is clearly documented in the figures. This is a key finding regarding climate independence.

result: The study demonstrates that mortality seasonality is largely similar in timing and magnitude across diverse climatic regions with substantially different temperatures, indicating that different regions in the USA are similarly adapted to temperature seasonality.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C70 synthesize the geographic findings from Figures 13-17. The inference about similar adaptation is reasonable given the data showing consistent seasonality despite temperature differences. This represents a major conclusion about the relationship between climate and mortality seasonality.

result: The decline in seasonal mortality differences in adolescents and young adults was related to diminishing seasonality of unintentional injuries, especially road traffic crashes (which peak in summer and are more common in men). The weakening seasonality in boys under 5 was related to declining seasonality of cardiorespiratory disease deaths and increasing proportion of deaths from perinatal conditions (which exhibit limited seasonality).
evaluation: Claims C73-C76 provide mechanistic explanations for temporal changes, stated in the Discussion with supporting citations and data from Figures 9-10 supplements and Figure 12 supplement 1. The explanations are consistent with the observed patterns and supported by the cause-specific decomposition.

result: Mortality in older ages maintained persistent seasonality over three decades. Although percent seasonal difference remained largely unchanged, the absolute difference in death rates between peak and minimum months declined because total mortality has a declining long-term trend.
evaluation: Claims C77-C78 describe the persistence of seasonality in older ages (Figures 1-2, 12) with an important clarification about absolute vs. relative differences. The distinction between percent and absolute differences is mathematically sound and important for interpretation.

result: Prior studies show mixed results on the relationship between temperature and mortality seasonality. A US study of 36 cities found no association between excess mortality and seasonal temperature range, while a European study found lower winter-summer mortality differences in colder Nordic countries than warmer southern European nations.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 accurately cite prior literature in the Discussion section. These provide context for interpreting the current study's findings. The citations are appropriately used to compare and contrast with the present results.

result: The authors speculate that Nordic countries may have better environmental and health system measures to counter cold winters than southern Europe, and that if the observed absence of association between mortality seasonality magnitude and temperature persists over time, climate change is unlikely to affect winter-summer mortality differences.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are speculative statements in the Discussion. C71 offers a plausible explanation for European patterns but lacks direct evidence. C72 makes a conditional prediction about climate change impacts that extends beyond the data. These are reasonable hypotheses but not directly tested.

result: The persistent seasonality in older populations demonstrates the need for environmental and health service interventions irrespective of geography and climate. Suggested interventions include better home insulation, winter heating provision, flu vaccinations, regular visits to isolated elderly during peak mortality periods, responsive emergency care, and emerging technologies like connected devices and sensors. Such interventions remain important as populations age and climate change increases weather variability.
evaluation: Claims C79-C83 present policy recommendations based on the finding of persistent seasonality in older ages (C77). The recommendations are reasonable applications of the findings, supported by citations (C80-C82). The forward-looking statement (C83) is a logical extension of the results.

result: A limitation of the study is that it did not investigate seasonality by socioeconomic characteristics, which may help understand determinants and plan responses.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 acknowledge a clear limitation explicitly stated in the Strengths and limitations section. This is an appropriate recognition of what the study did not address and represents good scientific practice.

result: The study used geo-coded mortality data from 1980-2016, wavelet analysis to detect seasonality, center of gravity analysis with circular statistics to identify timing of peaks, and ERA-Interim temperature data. Specific R packages (WaveletComp version 1.0, CircStats version 0.2.4) were used for analyses.
evaluation: Claims C86-C92 describe the methodological approach stated in the Abstract, Introduction, and Materials and methods sections. The methods are clearly documented with appropriate citations for wavelet analysis (C88) and ERA-Interim (C91-C92). Software versions are specified (C89-C90), supporting reproducibility.

result: The study builds on established knowledge that winter deaths exceed summer ones in temperate climates, that wavelets have been used to study weather and infectious diseases, and that mortality seasonality may vary geographically and temporally. It has been hypothesized that a warmer world may lower winter mortality.
evaluation: Claims C1, C45-C49 provide background context from the Introduction with appropriate citations. These establish the scientific foundation and motivation for the study. The claims accurately represent prior knowledge and hypotheses in the field.

result: The study analyzed nine distinct US climate regions with varying temperature characteristics. Injuries accounted for 8% of deaths in 1980 and 7.3% in 2016, and may have seasonality distinct from natural causes. The Southeast and South are hottest (18.4°C, 18°C average), while West North Central, East North Central, and Northwest are coldest (7.6-8.2°C). Temperature variation ranges from 17.5°C (Southeast) to 30.5°C (West North Central). The Northeast is most populous (19.8% of 2016 population).
evaluation: Claims C55-C65 provide descriptive information about the study design and climate regions from the Materials and methods section, supported by Figure 18 and Table 2. The temperature data and regional characteristics are clearly documented. The speculation about distinct injury seasonality (C57) is supported by subsequent results.

result: The study identified distinct seasonal patterns in relation to age and sex, including higher all-cause summer mortality in young men, using wavelet and center of gravity analyses.
evaluation: Claim C66 summarizes key findings stated in the Discussion with supporting citations. This accurately reflects the major patterns identified in the results (particularly C7, C34) and the methodological approach used.
